<STRUCT_0001>
Here is the definition of an algebraic stack. We remark that condition
(2) implies we can make sense out of the condition in part (3) that
<MATH_0001>
is smooth and surjective, see discussion following
Lemma <REF_0001>.

Let <MATH_0001> be a base scheme contained in <MATH_0002>.
An <TEXTITOPEN_0001>algebraic stack over <MATH_0003><TEXTITCLOSE_0001> is a category
<MATH_0004>
over <MATH_0005> with the following properties:
<STRUCT_0001>
<STRUCT_0002> The category <MATH_0006> is a stack in groupoids over
<MATH_0007>.
<STRUCT_0003> The diagonal
<MATH_0008>
is representable by algebraic spaces.
<STRUCT_0004> There exists a scheme <MATH_0009>
and a <MATH_0010>-morphism <MATH_0011>
which is surjective and smooth<FOOTNOTEOPEN_0001>In future chapters we will denote
this simply <MATH_0012> as is customary in the literature. Another
good alternative would be to formulate this condition as the existence of a
representable category fibred in groupoids <MATH_0013> and a surjective
smooth <MATH_0014>-morphism <MATH_0015>.<FOOTNOTECLOSE_0001>.
<STRUCT_0005>

<STRUCT_0001>
There are some differences with other definitions found in the literature.

<STRUCT_0002><STRUCT_0003>
The first is that we require <MATH_0001> to be a stack in groupoids
in the fppf topology, whereas in many references the <ACCENT_0001>tale topology is
used. It somehow seems to us that the fppf topology is the natural topology
to work with. In the end the resulting <MATH_0002>-category of algebraic stacks
ends up being the same. This is explained in
Criteria for Representability, Section <REF_0001>.

<STRUCT_0004><STRUCT_0005>
The second is that we only require the diagonal map of <MATH_0003> to be
representable by algebraic spaces, whereas in most references some other
conditions are imposed. Our point of view is to try to prove a certain
number of the results that follow only assuming that the diagonal
of <MATH_0004> be representable by algebraic spaces, and simply add
an additional hypothesis wherever this is necessary. It has the added
benefit that any algebraic space (as defined in
Spaces, Definition <REF_0002>)
gives rise to an algebraic stack.

<STRUCT_0006><STRUCT_0007>
The third is that in some papers it is required that there exists a
scheme <MATH_0005> and a surjective and <ACCENT_0002>tale morphism <MATH_0006>.
In the groundbreaking paper <REF_0003> where algebraic stacks were first
introduced Deligne and Mumford used this definition and showed that
the moduli stack of stable genus <MATH_0007> curves is an algebraic stack
which has an <ACCENT_0003>tale covering by a scheme. Michael Artin, see
<REF_0004>, realized that many
natural results on algebraic stacks generalize to the case where one
only assume a smooth covering by a scheme. Hence our choice above.
To distinguish the two cases one sees the terms ``Deligne-Mumford stack''
and ``Artin stack'' used in the literature. We will reserve the term
``Artin stack'' for later use (insert future reference here), and continue
to use ``algebraic stack'', but we will use ``Deligne-Mumford stack''
to indicate those algebraic stacks which have an <ACCENT_0004>tale covering by a
scheme.
